parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem: State, for an X-ray image, what is meant by:

markscheme_points.text: ease with which edges can be distinguished

hints: Hint 1: Picture a photograph of a bone - think about whether the boundary between bone and soft tissue looks crisp and clear or blurred and fuzzy.
parts.proper_answer: Sharpness is the ease with which the edges of structures can be distinguished on the image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Makes An Image Look Clear**
Think of sharpness just like a normal camera photo. A sharp photo lets you see exactly where one object ends and the next begins. In an X-ray, you are looking at shadows of bones and organs, so sharpness tells you how clearly you can trace the outline or edge of a structure.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the black and white areas on an X-ray film - think about what makes bone stand out strongly from the surrounding soft tissue.
parts.proper_answer: Contrast is the difference in degree of blackening between adjacent areas of the image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Black Versus White**
An X-ray film is a map of blackening. Where many X-rays get through, the film goes dark. Where they are absorbed, it stays light. Contrast is simply how big that difference in blackening is between two neighbouring regions, for example dense bone next to soft muscle. High contrast means very distinct light and dark areas.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A parallel X-ray beam passes through a thickness of $2.3\ \text{cm}$ of soft body tissue. The intensity of the emerging beam is $12\%$ of the intensity of the incident beam.

Calculate the linear attenuation (absorption) coefficient $\mu$ of the soft body tissue. Give a unit with your answer.
hints: Hint 1: Remember that X-ray intensity does not fall in a straight line with thickness - each equal extra thickness removes the same fraction of what is left.
Hint 2: Write the transmitted fraction $I/I_0 = 0.12$ with thickness $x = 2.3\text{ cm}$ into the exponential law and take natural logs on both sides to bring $\mu$ down.
Hint 3: Solve for $\mu = -\ln(0.12)/2.3$ and remember that $\mu \times x$ must be dimensionless, so check what unit $\mu$ must have.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **The Law That Governs Absorption**
You have a parallel beam losing intensity as it goes through tissue. The physics is exponential attenuation because photons are randomly absorbed or scattered. The governing law is $$I = I_0 \exp(-\mu x)$$ where $I_0$ is incident intensity, $I$ is transmitted intensity, $x$ is thickness and $\mu$ is the linear attenuation coefficient. A large $\mu$ means strongly absorbing material.

Step 2: **Put In The Numbers**
Here $x = 2.3\text{ cm}$ and the emerging intensity is 12% of the incident, so $$\frac{I}{I_0} = 0.12$$ Substituting: $$0.12 = \exp(-\mu \times 2.3)$$ To solve for $\mu$, take the natural log of both sides: $$\ln(0.12) = -2.3\mu$$

Step 3: **Calculate And Add The Unit**
$$\mu = \frac{-\ln(0.12)}{2.3} = \frac{2.12}{2.3} \approx 0.92$$ Since the exponent $\mu x$ has no units, $\mu$ has units of $1/\text{length}$. With $x$ in cm: $$\mu = 0.92\text{ cm}^{-1}$$ This is to 2 s.f., matching the data.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
In medical diagnosis, X-rays may be used to produce a single X-ray image or may be used in computed tomography (CT scanning).

Suggest an advantage and a disadvantage of CT scanning compared with single X-ray imaging for diagnosis.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what you get from one single shadow view compared with many views taken from all around the body and built up by computer.
Hint 2: Think about what taking many X-ray exposures from many angles must mean for the total radiation received by the patient.
parts.proper_answer: Advantage: CT scanning produces a detailed 3-dimensional image / cross-sectional slices, allowing soft tissues to be distinguished. Disadvantage: much greater radiation exposure / dose to the patient.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why CT Is More Powerful**
A single X-ray is just one flat 2D shadow where all the structures overlap. In CT, the tube rotates around you taking hundreds of slices from different angles, and the computer reconstructs them. That builds up a full 3D view and thin cross-sections, so you can see inside soft tissue and locate a tumour precisely, not just bones.

Step 2: **The Price You Pay**
All those extra views mean many more X-ray exposures. So the total ionising radiation dose is much larger than for a single film. That increases risk of cell damage, and the scan also takes longer, costs more and needs complex computing.
